title: Query optimisation: plan-space example
lead: The Reserves/Sailors example from the source slides, with the same data sizes and cost assumptions.

sections.title: Source query and selection pushdown
sections.html:
Query, cardinalities and buffer budget

SELECT S.sname
FROM Reserves AS R JOIN Sailors AS S ON R.sid=S.sid
WHERE R.bid=100 AND S.rating>5;

Reserves has 1000 pages×100 tuples=100,000 tuples at 40 bytes each. Sailors has 500 pages×80=40,000 tuples at 50 bytes each. Boat IDs are uniform over 100 values, so bid=100 retains 1000 tuples, about 10 packed pages. Ratings are uniform over 1…10, so rating>5 retains half, about 250 packed pages. B=5 frames leaves three outer frames for block NL.

These packed intermediate-page estimates do not mean matching tuples originally occupy only that many base pages. All costs below exclude final output writes and count each base scan once where it is pipelined.

PDF pp. 1–3

Plans 1 and 2: filter the outer input

Plan 1 joins full Sailors outside to full Reserves inside, then filters: 500+500·1000=500,500 I/Os. Moving rating>5 below the join means the outer stream is repacked to about 250 page-equivalents, while obtaining it still scans 500 source pages.

Plan 2 therefore costs 500+250·1000=250,500. Projection and selections on the result stream add CPU but no intermediate disk writes under the source’s on-the-fly assumption. The saving comes from fewer inner rescans, not from halving the original Sailors scan.

PDF pp. 4–9

Plan 3: why inner filtering saves no page reads

Push bid=100 onto the inner Reserves scan but do not materialise it. Each outer page still starts a new scan of all 1000 Reserves source pages to discover qualifying tuples. Cost remains 500+250·1000=250,500.

The inner filter reduces comparisons/output tuples after pages have been read. To reduce repeated source reads, change the access path or retain a reusable intermediate. This is a physical execution distinction that a logical pushdown diagram alone does not reveal.

PDF pp. 10–13

sections.title: Join order and materialisation
sections.html:
Plan 4: reverse the join orientation

Filter Reserves first and place it outside. Producing that stream scans 1000 pages; its approximately ten packed outer pages each trigger a 500-page Sailors scan. Total=1000+10·500=6000 I/Os.

Both relations are logically filtered, but they have different selectivities. Choosing the much smaller filtered outer input reduces the number of complete inner scans. The plan still rescans original Sailors pages because its filter remains on the fly.

PDF pp. 14–17

Plan 5: materialise filtered Sailors

Scan Sailors once (500), write its filtered T1 (250 pages), then scan those temporary pages ten times for filtered Reserves. Add the Reserves source scan (1000): 1000+500+250+10·250=4250 I/Os.

The 250 writes are a new cost, exchanged for cheaper repeated reads. Materialising the inner input makes its selectivity affect scan I/O; simply evaluating the predicate during every original scan did not.

PDF pp. 18–20

Plan 6: reverse with materialised Reserves

Materialise the ten-page filtered Reserves result instead. Stream filtered Sailors as the 250-page outer input. Cost=500 Sailors reads+1000 Reserves reads+10 temporary writes+250·10 temporary reads=4010.

Reversing a join changes its rescan count and the intermediate written, even when the same two filtered relations are joined. Compare complete ledgers, not just the sizes of the logical children.

PDF pp. 21–24

sections.title: Join algorithms and narrower tuples
sections.html:
Plan 7: streamed initial sorting

With five buffers, filtered Reserves’ ten pages form two initial runs and merge once: initial writes10 plus merge read/write20=30. Filtered Sailors’ 250 pages form 50 initial runs, then 13,4,1: initial writes250 plus three read/write passes of500=1750.

Base scans already provide initial sort input, so do not charge another initial read. Separate final join merge reads10+250=260. Total=1000+500+30+1750+260=3540. One later source panel prints 3510; the detailed ledger gives 3540, which is used consistently here.

PDF pp. 25–29

Plan 8: three-frame outer blocks

Keep Plan6’s materialised ten-page Reserves and switch the join to block NL. B−2=3 outer frames group the 250 Sailors page-equivalents into ceil(250/3)=84 blocks.

Each block scans ten T1 pages:840 reads. Base scans1500 plus temporary writes10 plus repeated reads840 give2350. Do not add another250 outer-page reads because Sailors is pipelined directly from the source scan/filter.

PDF pp. 30–33

Plan 9: projection changes the memory regime

Filtered Reserves contains1000 tuples×40 bytes=40,000 bytes, about ten source-sized pages. Retaining only 4-byte sid shrinks it to4000 bytes, about one packed page. Keep sid multiplicities: this is bag projection, not DISTINCT.

Place that one-page result outside and retain it in memory; scan Sailors once, testing rating and joining sid. No temporary materialisation is needed. Cost=1000+500=1500. This is the read-both-inputs bound in this no-index model, not a general lower bound with indexes or preexisting cache.

PDF pp. 34–38

sections.title: Indexed plan and comparison
sections.html:
Plan 10: cached indexes and unique probes

Assume a clustered index on Reserves.bid and an unclustered one on Sailors.sid, with index navigation resident. bid=100 fetches1000 records on ten clustered pages. Each sid probe finds at most one Sailors record and is charged one data-page read:10+1000·1=1010 I/Os.

Projecting outer fields away does not reduce the number of tuple probes, unlike reducing block-NL pages. Sailors.rating is not supplied by the sid-only index, so testing it requires the fetched record; moving the test in a diagram does not remove that read. If indexes are not cached or sid is nonunique, include the extra work.

PDF pp. 39–42

All ten alternatives in source order

PlanChangeI/O
1Unfiltered page NL500500
2Outer selection250500
3Inner on-the-fly selection250500
4Reverse orientation6000
5Materialise Sailors4250
6Materialise Reserves, reverse4010
7Sort-merge3540
8Block NL2350
9Project sid, fit outer1500
10Index NL1010

The sequence explores only part of the plan space. Every reduction follows a specific change to access, rescan count, tuple width, buffering or temporary writes; logical equivalence alone does not determine I/O.

PDF p. 43

quiz.question: Does filtering an inner heap from 600 pages to 12 output pages automatically reduce each scan to 12 I/Os?
options: No, if each scan still reads the 600-page heap
It depends only on the number of SELECT columns
quiz.explanation: Output size and the number of input pages that must be read are different quantities.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes repeated plan refinement; selection pushdown inside and outside nested loops; join orientation; materializing filtered inner input; sort-merge pass accounting; block nested loops and projection width; and clustered outer access with an indexed inner join. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
